title: Selection Bias in Hybrid Randomized Controlled Trials using External Controls: A Simulation Study
extended_summary:
This paper investigates a methodological problem in clinical-trial statistics: how bias can be introduced in hybrid randomized controlled trials when investigators selectively choose which historical or external control datasets to borrow from. The central question is whether outcome-dependent selection of external controls can distort treatment effect estimates, statistical power, and type I error rates, even when modern frequentist and Bayesian borrowing methods such as test-then-pool and robust MAP priors are used.

The authors study this question through simulation rather than an educational intervention. They simulate hybrid RCTs with binary outcomes, varying between-trial heterogeneity, number and size of historical studies, sample sizes of prospective trials, randomization ratios, and scenarios involving exchangeability, prior-data conflict, and time trends. They compare several external-control selection rules, including full selection, random selection, drop-the-best, threshold-based selection, and optimal-power selection. A clinical case study in ankylosing spondylitis is also used to illustrate how these selection rules affect inference in practice.

There is no student, teacher, school, or education population in this paper. The context is biostatistics and clinical trial methodology, with simulations conducted by researchers at the Medical University of Vienna and a case study based on a medical trial. The paper does discuss randomized controlled trials conceptually, but the main contribution is not a primary randomized experiment with human participants in an educational setting; it is a simulation study of statistical properties under different assumptions and selection mechanisms.

The main conclusion is that outcome-dependent selection of external controls can substantially inflate type I error, increase bias, and overstate treatment effects, while offering only modest gains in power. Full or random prespecified selection is more conservative and less biased. The authors argue that external-control sources should be prespecified and transparently justified, and that outcome-dependent selection undermines the validity of both Bayesian and frequentist inference. This paper is not the alleged 2026 high-school ChatGPT writing motivation trial and should not be included in a quantitative synthesis of ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school.
quality_tier_rationale: This is not an education intervention study and contains no K-12 or writing-related empirical evaluation. It is an arXiv methodological simulation paper about selection bias in hybrid clinical randomized controlled trials using external controls, so it is not relevant evidence for ChatGPT-based writing feedback.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no educational intervention effects, no student motivation outcomes, and no writing outcomes. It therefore provides no usable impact evidence for a synthesis on ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school.
